1201|  truth; the Redis `alerts:active:<symbol>` key stays what it was introduced for

1204|- **Comparison.** `PriceThresholdEvaluator` compares exact `Decimal` values and
1205|  the boundaries are inclusive: `ABOVE` fires on `price >= threshold`, `BELOW`
1206|  on `price <= threshold`, so a print exactly on the target fires. A rule whose
1207|  threshold is missing or not a finite number is disabled rather than defaulted
1208|  to zero (which would fire on every tick).
1209|- **Cooldown (default 1 hour).** Checked twice: first against the Redis marker
1210|  `alert:cooldown:<alert_id>` (written with `SETEX`, so the window expires on its
1211|  own) to keep the common "condition still true on the next tick" case off the
1212|  database, then against `alert_rules.last_triggered` after the row is locked.
1213|  The second check is authoritative, so a Redis outage - or two price updates
1214|  racing for the same alert - still triggers only once.
1215|- **One transaction per trigger.** `SELECT ... FOR UPDATE` re-reads the rule, a
1216|  rule deleted or paused mid-evaluation is skipped, `last_triggered` is set, the
1217|  `AlertTriggered` event is published to `alerts`, and only then is the
1218|  transaction committed. Publishing before the commit means a broker failure
1219|  rolls `last_triggered` back and the next price update retries, rather than the
1220|  alert being silently swallowed. The same commit also writes the
1221|  `alert_history` row, so the durable record of what the user was told cannot
1222|  diverge from the trigger that told them (see the TASK-21 section below).
1223|- **Stale and malformed input.** Prices older than `ALERT_MAX_PRICE_AGE_SECONDS`
1224|  (default 300) are ignored, since acting on a delayed tick would fire at a price
1225|  the market has already left. An unparseable timestamp counts as "age unknown"
1226|  and is evaluated. Each rule is evaluated in its own try/except so one bad rule
1227|  cannot stop the rest of the symbol's alerts, and every evaluation is logged at
1228|  debug level so a non-firing alert can be distinguished from one never evaluated.

1235|Alert Engine Service - As Built (TASK-19):
1236|
1237|Moving-average crossovers are realised in
1238|`services/alert-engine/app/moving_average.py` (`MovingAverageCalculator` and
1239|`MovingAverageEngine`), with the detection itself in `MovingAverageEvaluator`
1240|(`app/evaluators.py`) and the Redis primitives in `app/state.py`. The points
1241|that matter:
1242|
1243|- **Buffers are bounded by the window they serve.** Each symbol/period pair owns
1244|  one Redis list, `ma:{symbol}:{period}` (section 3.2.4): `LPUSH` the new price,
1245|  `LTRIM` it to `period` entries. The average of the last 50 prices needs exactly
1246|  50 of them, so a symbol ticking once a second holds 50 values rather than an
1247|  ever-growing history. Prices are only recorded for symbols that have an active
1248|  moving-average rule, so no unread buffer is ever created.
1249|- **A crossover is an edge, never a level.** `GOLDEN_CROSS` fires on
1250|  `previous_short < previous_long and current_short > current_long`, and
1251|  `DEATH_CROSS` on the mirror transition. Comparing levels - "is the short
1252|  average above the long one?" - would re-fire on every tick for as long as the
1253|  trend lasted, which is what this replaces.
1254|- **Averages are withheld until the window is full.** An average of three of the
1255|  twenty prices it is meant to cover is not a twenty-period average, so nothing
1256|  is reported until `long_period` prices have been observed. The first full
1257|  window is a *baseline*: with no previous averages there is a starting state,
1258|  not a crossing, so a freshly created rule cannot fire on a trend that predates
1259|  it.
1260|- **The baseline lives in Redis and advances only after a completed
1261|  evaluation.** `ma:snapshot:{symbol}:{short}:{long}` holds the previous averages
1262|  and their timestamp, so a restart does not lose the comparison and two rules
1263|  sharing a window both compare against the last tick rather than against each
1264|  other's freshly written values. If a trigger raises - the broker rejects the
1265|  event - the baseline is deliberately *not* advanced, so the crossover is still
1266|  pending on the next tick instead of vanishing with the failed publish.
1267|- **Everything after the decision is shared.** The cooldown (Redis marker plus
1268|  `alert_rules.last_triggered`), the row-locked transaction, the Redis trigger
1269|  history and the `AlertTriggered` event shape are the TASK-18 machinery in
1270|  `app/triggering.py`, so both engines trigger identically and a crossover is
1271|  subject to the same one-hour cooldown.

1273|  prices parsed through `str()`, so a cross that exists only beyond float64
1274|  precision is still detected. A gap in the history contributes fewer
1275|  observations, never interpolated ones: the window is the last *N observed*
1276|  prices. A stale tick is discarded before it can enter a buffer at all, and if
1277|  the buffers cannot be read the engine stays silent rather than alerting on a
1278|  window it cannot see.

1284|Percentage-Change Alerts - As Built (TASK-20):
1285|
1286|Percentage-change alerts are realised in `services/alert-engine/app/percentage_change.py`
1287|(`HistoricalPriceProvider` and `PercentageChangeEngine`), with the arithmetic and the
1288|direction rules in `PercentageChangeEvaluator` (`app/evaluators.py`) and the Redis
1289|cache in `app/state.py`. These are the parts worth knowing:
1290|
1291|- **The reference is historical, and comes from `ohlcv_candles`.** A
1292|  percentage-change alert does not measure a move from the first price observed
1293|  after it was armed; it measures it over its *timeframe*, so the engine resolves
1294|  the far end of the window itself from the pre-aggregated candles (section 3.2.3,
1295|  `percentage_change_pipeline`) and hands it to the evaluator. The query is the
1296|  newest candle at or before the reference instant, which is also how a window
1297|  ending on a weekend, a holiday or outside market hours resolves to the last
1298|  price the market actually printed instead of to nothing.
1299|- **The reference is the candle that had already closed.** A candle's timestamp
1300|  marks its *open* while the price it contributes is its *close*, one interval
1301|  later, so `now - timeframe` is floored to the candle grid *and* shifted back one
1302|  interval (`reference_instant`). Without that shift a `24h` alert would measure
1303|  from the close of a session that had not finished yet, and report a move far
1304|  smaller than the one the user asked about. Timeframes map to intervals as
1305|  `1h -> 1h`, `24h -> 1d`, `7d -> 1d`.
1306|- **Direction.** `UP` fires on a rise of at least `threshold_percent`, `DOWN` on a
1307|  fall of at least that size, and `BOTH` on a move of that size in either
1308|  direction - the volatility case, which compares `abs(percentage_change)`. A
1309|  price that has not moved cannot fire, because the threshold must be positive for
1310|  the rule to be usable at all. A zero stored close is logged and skipped rather
1311|  than treated as a move of infinity.
1312|- **One lookup per timeframe per tick.** Three alerts on the same `24h` window
1313|  share a single historical read; the results are cached in Redis under
1314|  `pct:reference:{symbol}:{timeframe}:{candle}`. The key embeds the candle bucket,
1315|  so a cached value cannot go stale while it lives, and the TTL only bounds the
1316|  number of keys. A Redis failure costs a MongoDB query per tick; a MongoDB
1317|  failure, or a symbol with less history than the timeframe needs, skips that
1318|  alert and leaves every other alert on the symbol alone.
1319|- **The event carries the move.** `AlertTriggered` for this rule type adds
1320|  `percentage_change` (signed, as a percentage) alongside the six shared fields,
1321|  so a notification can say "AAPL is up 8.4% in the last 24h". The other rule types
1322|  do not carry the field.
1323|- **Everything after the decision is shared.** The cooldown, the row-locked
1324|  transaction, the `alert_history` row and the event shape are the TASK-18
1325|  machinery in `app/triggering.py`, so all three engines trigger identically.

1328|Alert History - As Built (TASK-21):
1329|
1330|Trigger history is a Postgres table (``AlertHistory`` in
1331|`services/alert-engine/app/models.py`), written by the trigger pipeline, read by
1332|`services/alert-engine/app/history.py` and exposed by the two history routes in
1333|`services/alert-engine/app/routers/alerts.py`. The points that matter:
1334|
1335|- **The row is written by the trigger, not by a listener.** `_trigger` stages the
1336|  `alert_history` entry in the same transaction that sets `last_triggered` and
1337|  publishes `AlertTriggered`, so the three cannot disagree: a trigger rolled back
1338|  by a broker failure leaves no history row claiming the user was notified. This
1339|  replaced the bounded per-alert and per-user Redis lists the earlier engines
1340|  kept, which had become a second copy of the record that could diverge from the
1341|  database and had no reader once the API was database-backed.
1342|- **The row is self-contained.** Symbol, rule type, rule name and the
1343|  configuration *as evaluated* are copied onto the row rather than joined from
1344|  `alert_rules`, so editing or deleting a rule cannot rewrite the history it
1345|  already produced. `alert_id` is the one link back and is `ON DELETE SET NULL`:
1346|  deleting a rule keeps the triggers it fired, they simply stop pointing at a
1347|  live rule. The user-wide route then reports `alert_id: null` while the per-alert
1348|  route is a 404, because there is no longer a rule whose ownership to check.
1349|- **Both routes are paginated and filterable.** `page`/`per_page` (default 20),
1350|  `symbol`, `rule_type` and `date_from`/`date_to` as inclusive instants, ordered
1351|  `trigger_time DESC` with `id` breaking ties so paging cannot repeat or skip a
1352|  row. Bounds are converted to UTC before they reach the driver, so one bound
1353|  means the same instant on SQLite (which stores naive datetimes) and on Postgres.
1354|  A reversed range is a 400 rather than an empty page, which a client would
1355|  otherwise read as "you have no history".
1356|- **Scoped in the query, not only in the handler.** Every read filters on
1357|  `user_id` in addition to the router's ownership check, so a future caller that
1358|  forgets the check still cannot read another user's history.
1359|- **Retention runs in-process.** `AlertHistoryService.purge_expired` deletes rows
1360|  older than `ALERT_HISTORY_RETENTION_DAYS` (default 365), driven by a task in
1361|  `app/main.py` at startup and then every
1362|  `ALERT_HISTORY_PURGE_INTERVAL_SECONDS` (default 86400). The delete is
1363|  idempotent, so replicas may run it concurrently, and a non-positive window or
1364|  interval turns the policy off without affecting the endpoints.
1365|- **`alert_rules.name`** is the optional label (max 120 characters) the history
1366|  response names the alert by; it is snapshotted into `rule_name` when a trigger
1367|  fires, so a later rename does not relabel old triggers.

1371|Price Consumer - As Built (TASK-22):
1372|
1373|The Kafka consumer of section 5.1 is realised by `AlertEngineConsumer` in
1374|`services/alert-engine/app/consumer.py`, on top of
1375|`stockvisor_shared.messaging.PriceConsumer` and the loop in
1376|`stockvisor_shared.kafka.KafkaConsumerManager`. It is the one place where the
1377|design's `PriceConsumer.process_price_updates` / `evaluate_alerts` split is
1378|implemented: the loop is shared plumbing, the per-message semantics are the
1379|alert engine's.
1380|
1381|- **One rule load per price update.** `evaluate_alerts` loads *all* of the
1382|  symbol's active rules in a single query
1383|  (`app.triggering.load_active_rules_for_symbol`), groups them by `rule_type` and
1384|  hands each engine its own group. Without it the three engines would each run
1385|  their own query for the same tick. A rule type no engine evaluates is logged
1386|  and skipped rather than silently ignored.
1387|- **Concurrent evaluation, bounded.** Every alert for the symbol is evaluated as
1388|  its own `asyncio.gather` task (the three engines also run together), capped by
1389|  one semaphore shared by all three engines - so
1390|  `ALERT_MAX_CONCURRENT_EVALUATIONS` (default 100) is a property of the service,
1391|  not of a rule type - and each task is bounded by
1392|  `ALERT_EVALUATION_TIMEOUT_SECONDS` (default 30) so one stuck database call
1393|  cannot hold a batch past `max.poll.interval.ms`. A failed or timed-out
1394|  evaluation is logged against its rule and the others still run; cancellation
1395|  from a shutdown is *not* absorbed. See `app/evaluation_concurrency.py`.
1396|- **Commit only after processing.** The consumer sets `enable_auto_commit=False`
1397|  and commits **explicit** offsets derived from the records it has actually
1398|  handled. That distinction is the whole point: aiokafka's bare `commit()`
1399|  commits the *fetch* position, which has already run past records sitting in the
1400|  client's buffer that the handler never saw. A message routed to the DLQ counts
1401|  as handled and is committed (otherwise a poison message replays forever); if
1402|  the DLQ publish itself fails the offset is deliberately left uncommitted, so a
1403|  message is never both unprocessed and unrecoverable.
1404|- **`alerts-dlq`, not the shared `dead-letter-queue`.** A price update that
1405|  cannot be processed is quarantined for the alert engine alone, with its topic,
1406|  partition, offset, original payload, error type and consumer group.
1407|- **Malformed payloads are skipped, not fatal.** `value_deserializer` degrades a
1408|  decode failure to a `MalformedMessage` instead of raising, because an exception
1409|  in the fetch path takes the entire iteration down over one bad record. The loop
1410|  logs it, dead-letters it, commits and carries on.
1411|- **Backpressure by pausing, with hysteresis.** Lag is checked every
1412|  `ALERT_CONSUMER_LAG_CHECK_INTERVAL_SECONDS`; above
1413|  `ALERT_CONSUMER_MAX_LAG_BEFORE_PAUSE` (5000) every assigned partition is
1414|  paused, and it resumes below `ALERT_CONSUMER_RESUME_LAG_RATIO` (0.8) of that
1415|  mark. Two thresholds rather than one so the consumer does not flap while the
1416|  lag sits on the boundary. Pausing - rather than dropping records - keeps the
1417|  partitions owned while evaluation catches up. The same lag snapshot feeds the
1418|  `kafka_consumer_lag` Prometheus metric, so the exported number and the pause
1419|  decision cannot disagree. Other services pass no threshold and are unaffected.
1420|- **Graceful shutdown finishes the batch.** `stop()` sets the stop flag and
1421|  *waits*; the loop completes the records it already fetched, commits them, and
1422|  only then disconnects. Cancelling the task instead - the previous behaviour -
1423|  would replay the whole batch on the next start. `main.py` therefore stops the
1424|  consumer before cancelling its task.
1425|- **Rebalances are handled, not ignored.** A `ConsumerRebalanceListener` is
1426|  registered explicitly (the constructor's implicit subscribe has none). On
1427|  revocation the offsets that were handled but not yet committed are dropped and
1428|  logged by name; committing from inside the callback would re-enter the
1429|  coordinator that is running it. The new owner re-reads those records, and the
1430|  duplicate delivery is absorbed by the trigger's own `last_triggered` guard -
1431|  manual offset commit gives at-least-once consumption, and exactly-once
1432|  *notification* is enforced where it belongs, in the trigger transaction.
1433|- **Outages are ridden out.** `start()` retries with exponential backoff, a fetch
1434|  failure reconnects and keeps the loop alive (bounded by
1435|  `ALERT_CONSUMER_MAX_CONSECUTIVE_ERRORS`), and `process_price_updates` wraps the
1436|  loop in a supervisor so alert evaluation cannot stop silently for the lifetime
1437|  of the process. Startup runs in the background, so a Kafka outage does not hold
1438|  the API's readiness.
1439|- **`GET /health/consumer`** reports the consumer's own state, the live lag and
1440|  the backpressure decision: `disabled` (no brokers configured) and `degraded`
1441|  (paused, or a dead-letter/commit failure) answer 200, `unhealthy` (asked to run
1442|  and not running) answers 503. `/health` stays the process liveness check, and
1443|  the endpoint answers from a snapshot that makes no broker calls - which is
1444|  exactly when someone is asking.
1445|- **Per-message latency is both logged and measured.** Every message logs its
1446|  latency (debug, or a warning above the slow threshold), each batch logs its
1447|  record count, total latency and slowest message, and
1448|  `kafka_consumer_message_processing_seconds` exposes the distribution; the
1449|  counters `kafka_consumer_messages_processed_total` (handled / dead_lettered /
1450|  failed) and `kafka_consumer_rebalances_total` complete the picture.
